label: Mystery / detective
description: A fair-play puzzle: a crime, a detective, suspects with motives, clues and red herrings, and a reveal that the reader could have solved.
voice: First or third person, past tense, with the detective's observations precise and specific.
Clues are shown to the reader when the detective sees them, fairly.
Every suspect has a motive, a secret and a lie.
Interviews are duels; people lie for their own reasons, not only the killer.
Chapters end on a new clue, a new body or a lie exposed.

structure.guide: The crime is discovered, with one odd detail.
The detective takes the case, for a personal reason.
The suspects introduced, each with a motive.
structure.then: Interviews and clues; each chapter one lie exposed.

structure.guide: A second crime or reversal that kills the leading theory.
The detective (or police) accuses the wrong person.
The gathering and the reveal, using clues the reader saw.
The aftermath and what it cost.

outline_guidance: Each chapter should contain at least one concrete clue or one exposed lie, named in the line.
outline_example: The Clock in the Hall | At Wren House the morning after the party, Inspector Adaeze Obi notices the hall clock was wound backwards | The butler's alibi now depends on a time that never happened | The victim's niece asks to speak to her alone
scene_guidance: Keep a list of who knew what when.
worldbuilding: The true sequence of the crime, minute by minute
naming: Names that fit the setting and are easy to tell apart.
cliches: you'll never get away with this
sample:
The hall clock said twenty past nine.

Adaeze checked her own watch. Ten past eleven.

"Stopped?" said Constable Hale.

"No." She opened the case with a gloved finger. The key was still warm from someone's pocket. "Wound. Backwards."
